units.passage: The challenge is to help CS students learn the fundamental concepts of CS without relying on AI, then to use AI to in their productivity to prepare them for a workforce that expects them to use AI tools.
units.why: The challenge is to teach 'fundamental concepts of CS without relying on AI'; fundamentals-first rationale for novices, so P42.

units.passage: In Computer Science, fundamental courses prioritize fundamental skill development (coding, analysis, problem solving, breaking down problems, debugging and testing, conceptual understanding) which are core skills that remain critical for students to be able to individually demonstrate.
units.why: 'fundamental courses prioritize fundamental skill development' that students must 'individually demonstrate' is the fundamentals-first rationale (P42).

units.passage: CS 321 Data Structures – GenAI should be carefully managed to allow students an introduction to appropriate use while continuing to restrict it for foundational computer science concepts.
units.why: CS 321: GenAI 'continuing to restrict it for foundational computer science concepts' keeps restriction for fundamentals (P42).

units.passage: This approach is because research has shown that unrestricted AI use can hinder learning for beginners
units.why: "research has shown that unrestricted AI use can hinder learning for beginners" is the reason for less AI in intro courses, protecting novices (P42).
units.fit_note: Cites research but gives no source in the text (B). (Coder notes: Cites research but gives no source in the text.)

units.passage: introductory courses like CS 2000 and CS 2100 will emphasize learning and practicing the fundamentals of program design and implementation, with only a brief introduction to the types of tasks AI can do
units.why: "introductory courses ... will emphasize learning and practicing the fundamentals of program design and implementation, with only a brief introduction to the types of tasks AI can do" is a course-design choice that puts fundamentals first and holds AI to a brief introduction (P42) in intro courses; instructor, before-course, informs, restrict.

units.passage: Effective usage of AI programming assistants requires humans with the ability to specify programs, validate that they do the right thing, and provide constructive feedback to improve them,
units.why: "Effective usage of AI programming assistants requires humans with the ability to specify programs, validate that they do the right thing" says novices need skills to judge AI output, P42.
units.fit_note: Also supports fundamentals-first (P42). / Also P31: validating AI output.

units.passage: In cases where you answer no, you may find yourself writing things like this: “I want my students to be able to edit writing without any assistance from AI. units.why: Example reasoning for a "no": "They won't be able to evaluate the suggestions AI would make unless they have their own strongly developed sense" says learners without skill cannot judge AI output, matching P42.
units.fit_note: Illustrative example of an instructor's rationale for no AI in an editing skill, not a university rule.

units.passage: The knowledge we’re teaching in this course is fundamental - you need to know it to be able to accomplish more complex tasks later.
units.why: Sample reason 'The knowledge we're teaching in this course is fundamental - you need to know it to be able to accomplish more complex tasks later' justifies no-use by fundamentals: P42. units.passage: The knowledge we’re teaching in this course is fundamental - you need to know it to be able to accomplish more complex tasks later.” “Generative AI tools hallucinate and aren’t trained to be truthful. So, in order to use generative AI output, you need this fundamental knowledge to know when the output is incorrect.”
units.why: Suggested wording: the knowledge 'is fundamental' and students need it 'to know when the output is incorrect'; fundamentals first, P42.

units.passage: If you have used a code generator to generate your code and do not understand how to code, you will not learn the skills necessary to know how to debug your code. If you ask for coding help and you cannot explain your code, the course staff will not be able to assist you.
units.why: "used a code generator to generate your code and do not understand how to code" warns that novices who skip coding cannot debug, which is the fundamentals-first point (P42).

units.passage: Without learning to accomplish tasks manually, students may not be able to learn to judge the quality of a GenAI’s output.
units.policy: Without learning to accomplish tasks manually, students may not be able to learn to judge the quality of a GenAI’s output.
units.why: Argues that without manual practice students 'may not be able to learn to judge the quality' of output: the novices-need-fundamentals argument (P42).

units.passage: This class is about basic concepts and skills and how to apply them and communicate them. If they use AI to figure out how to analyze some policy, or communicate the analysis, they are not learning that for themselves. They need to learn how to do 100% of the work themselves.
units.why: 'They need to learn how to do 100% of the work themselves' because the class teaches basic concepts; fundamentals first, P42.

units.passage: if they do not understand the basics fully they will never be able to harness the power of AI as an assistant effectively and responsibly.
units.policy: if they do not understand the basics fully they will never be able to harness the power of AI as an assistant effectively and responsibly.
units.why: Says without the basics students cannot use AI 'effectively and responsibly': fundamentals first (P42).

units.passage: o AI outputs cannot be judged well by those learning a field. o Students need to develop their research skills in their field of study to be able to assess AI’s output.
units.why: 'AI outputs cannot be judged well by those learning a field': novices cannot judge output, P42.

units.passage: Academic programs at Mines are invited to engage with alumni, industry, and community partners to consider which skills and knowledge are foundational and should not be outsourced to AI, and which tasks may be intentionally offloaded to free up mental capacity for higher-order thinking and creativity
units.why: Programs invited to consider 'which skills and knowledge are foundational and should not be outsourced to AI'; fundamentals first (P42).

units.passage: Many foundational skills will still need to be developed without the use of GAI.
units.why: The report states 'Many foundational skills will still need to be developed without the use of GAI.' This protects fundamentals first, so P42.

units.passage: To prohibit the use of GAI where it interferes with the student developing foundational understanding, skills, and knowledge needed for future courses and careers.
units.why: The first kind is 'To prohibit the use of GAI where it interferes with the student developing foundational understanding'. It is a conditional prohibition tied to foundational skills, so P42; P01 does not fit because it is not a default ban.

units.passage: We recommend educating students on the capabilities and limitations of these systems, prohibiting their use where basic skills need to be developed, and encouraging their use in cases where LLMs can improve student learning.
units.why: The report recommends 'prohibiting their use where basic skills need to be developed'. It is a conditional prohibition for foundational skills, so P42.
units.fit_note: Distinguishes by course goals rather than strictly by time.

units.passage: Prohibiting Generative AI Use in Your Course ( AI-FREE ) "To ensure development and mastery of the foundational concepts and skills in this course, the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools is prohibited.
units.why: The sample gives the reason: 'To ensure development and mastery of the foundational concepts and skills in this course'. Fundamentals first, so P42.

units.passage: The need for these skills will never become irrelevant.
units.why: Says foundational skills 'will never become irrelevant', supporting the priority of fundamentals; nearest P42, though not specific to novices.
units.fit_note: Claims lasting need for foundational skills; not about beginners specifically.

units.passage: you need to understand/apply fundamental concepts and skills without the use of AI tools
units.why: Alternate rationale: 'you need to understand/apply fundamental concepts and skills without the use of AI tools'; P42 fits as it argues fundamentals are needed before higher-level work.

units.passage: Generative AI is an important tool, but it is most effective when combined with strong foundational knowledge and critical thinking skills
units.why: 'most effective when combined with strong foundational knowledge and critical thinking skills' links good AI use to fundamentals; partly P42 (fundamentals first) but does not say novices must avoid AI.

units.passage: Similarly, a first-year student building foundational skills and judgment stands in a different relationship to AI than doctoral candidates accelerating literature review in a field they deeply know.
units.why: Contrasts a first-year student 'building foundational skills' with doctoral candidates, supporting differential treatment of novices, so P42.

units.passage: Students new to a discipline are likely to over-estimate AI’s accuracy and usefulness, and will need careful guidance and education to develop AI critical thinking.
units.policy: Students new to a discipline are likely to over-estimate AI's accuracy and usefulness, and will need careful guidance and education to develop AI critical thinking.
units.why: "Students new to a discipline are likely to over-estimate AI's accuracy" and "will need careful guidance and education"; novices cannot judge AI output, so P42 rather than P31 because the focus is on beginners.

units.passage: If your course is a lower-level course heavily focused on learning the terminology and underlying theory of your discipline, you may want to have a more prohibitive AI policy than an upper-level course focused on completing complex projects and engaging in experiential learning.
units.why: 'a lower-level course ... you may want to have a more prohibitive AI policy than an upper-level course' says beginners' courses need stricter AI limits, P42.

units.passage: Does your AI policy ensure that students learn the basic theories, concepts, and terminology deeply enough that they can use them in coursework, conversation, and future learning experiences?
units.why: 'students learn the basic theories, concepts, and terminology deeply enough' asks that the policy protect foundational learning, P42.
units.fit_note: Frames fundamentals as a policy-design check without mentioning novices or beginners.

units.passage: While AI is readily available and can be useful in some circumstances, it is essential that you learn basic skills to help you identify what good writing looks like before you’ll be able to accurately and ethically employ their use.
units.why: 'you learn basic skills ... before you'll be able to accurately and ethically employ their use' says fundamentals come before AI, P42.

units.passage: Students should master the fundamentals of their discipline through independent thinking

units.passage: Focus on developing foundational skills that are not dependent on AI technologies.
units.why: Reason offered for prohibition: 'Focus on developing foundational skills that are not dependent on AI technologies'. Fundamentals first: P42.

units.passage: It is critical for students to develop core research and writing skills first before adding AI
units.why: Ontario Tech: 'It is critical for students to develop core research and writing skills first before adding AI'; fundamentals first, P42.

units.passage: Most courses emphasize developing a strong foundation before advanced tool use.
units.why: "Most courses emphasize developing a strong foundation before advanced tool use" says fundamentals come first (P42).

units.passage: Use AI tools only for tasks that are appropriate for your level of learning and understanding.
units.why: "Use AI tools only for tasks that are appropriate for your level of learning" limits use by learner level; nearest is P42, which is about protecting novices.
units.fit_note: Leaves the judgment of what suits the student level to the student; no stated novice rationale. | Limits AI by the student's own level of understanding, which the type only implies.

units.passage: whereas they may need to avoid its use to acquire foundational knowledge and skills
units.why: Students "may need to avoid its use to acquire foundational knowledge and skills" gives the reason that fundamentals come first without AI, P42.

units.why: "students need to master foundational proficiencies" is given as a case where AI is not advisable, so the rationale that novices build fundamentals without AI (P42).
